## §3 Places

### The Administrative Block *(place · 3 pencil · 1 GM-only)*

`the-administrative-block`

**What people know**

- `the-administrative-block.the-ladder` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Administrative Block in Island Centre stacks the Directorate's ranks in one six-storey building: typewriters and telephones at the bottom, offices in the middle, and at the top a corridor where the floor stops being lino and becomes carpet. Each landing is quieter than the one below. The Section Officer works there, and so does the man two rungs above him. Candidates never go to the top floor, so being summoned there is the event before a word is said. People are left to wait on a bench outside a closed door, and the Section Officer waits on it too. — known some · told later · source D076, D081
- `the-administrative-block.the-establishment` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Establishment Offices, five storeys beside the Administrative Block and subordinate to it, hold the establishment: the list of who exists to the Directorate. Every candidate, every posting and every screening result is filed there by somebody who has never met them, so a person's file has a real address. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-administrative-block.decided-upstairs` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* What is decided on the top floor arrives downstairs as a duty change nobody explains, and is read on the muster yard's board before anyone says it was about them. — known few · told later · source D076

### Baldwin Manor *(place · 9 pencil · 7 GM-only)*

`baldwin-manor`

**What people know**

- `baldwin-manor.the-curious-child` *(Pencil · hers)* The Inicrium battery was made by a mitflit savant child who was just curious. When it was turned on, the town below the castle was overrun by shadow-plane creatures and the castle came under siege; the four worked out how to disable the generator by destroying it, and the shadows retreated. It has nothing to do with the exotic matter. — known some · told later · source D078, D006, D029
- `baldwin-manor.far-from-the-ship` *(Pencil · hers)* Baldwin Manor and the ruined generation ship are many miles apart. First Impact happened many miles from the manor, in a hidden, jungle-like valley on Kortos, and the two events are not to be confused. — known some · told later · source D078, D031

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `baldwin-manor.volkheed` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Baldwin Manor stands above the village of Volkheed on the Isle of Kortos, which was founded in 4071 AR. Inicrium mining began there around 4171 AR. — known nobody · told later · when 4071 AR · source D074, D029
- `baldwin-manor.mitflit-clan` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A mitflit clan arrived in Volkheed in 4147 AR and lent its "enigmatic skills and innate magical talents" to the Inicrium trade, becoming part of the village. — known nobody · told later · when 4147 AR · source D074, D029
- `baldwin-manor.croglang` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Inicrium trade paid for a castle, Croglang Castle, which the powerful Baldwin family later claimed and renamed Baldwin Manor. The old history's own dates are inconsistent: the castle is built in 4221 AR and renamed in 4201 AR. — known nobody · told later · when 4201 AR · source D074, D029
- `baldwin-manor.manufactory` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Baldwin Manor grew into one of the largest magical-weapons manufactories on Kortos, exporting across the sea to Absalom. A profits report for 4721 AR puts the year's net profit at about two hundred thousand gold pieces, a little lower that midsummer for fewer exports and fewer war contracts. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D029
- `baldwin-manor.the-family` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Baldwins at the manor were Alastair, a powerful fire caster; Castria Anne, an ice-and-water enchanter; Agatha Laine and Reginald Cavil; and William Charles Baldwin, the hunters' leader. The manor's Master Enchanter was Castria Anne Baldwin, who signed its materials procurement records: mithral, adamantine, cold iron, darkwood and drakescale by the hundredweight, bought from suppliers across the region, with a note about "enchantment surges for upcoming ceremony." — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D029, D081
- `baldwin-manor.the-siege` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* An Inicrium battery at the manor pulled the Shadow Plane into the town, and shadow creatures overran it. The four disabled the battery, and the shadows stopped encroaching. Members of the Baldwin family died in the siege, by accident and not at the four's hands. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D029, D031
- `baldwin-manor.the-dark-secret` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The GM's plan for the manor was that its people would not be innocent: a castle that invites the four in, a siege, and a dark secret in ritual sacrifice of prisoners, "both sides are fantatics". — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D029

### The Candidate Gate *(place · 3 pencil)*

`candidate-gate`

**What people know**

- `candidate-gate.signs-in-and-out` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Candidate Gate is the single staffed checkpoint at the housing rows' only road entrance. Every candidate signs in and out there, badge checked against a roster, curfew logged. The gate's ledger is the one honest record of who was outside the rows and when: any night out becomes a line in a book somebody can later read, and a breach logged there can't be talked away. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D081
- `candidate-gate.paperwork-and-proctors` *(Pencil · Claude)* At the gate the roster is always ahead of the person: candidates are expected before they arrive and logged before they speak, and the proctor reads a name off the roster before it is given. Nobody there is watching anybody; the Directorate is simply better at paperwork than at people. The off-duty proctors spend most of their shift under the gate's weather-beaten awning talking rather than checking anyone. They are bored, they are not officers, and they know the housing rows' gossip better than anyone with a rank. — known some · told later · source D076, D082
- `candidate-gate.the-corrected-figure` *(Pencil · Claude)* On the board screwed to the barrier post, somebody once corrected the second curfew figure by hand, and the board was never reprinted: the Directorate doesn't repaint signs. It means nothing more. — known everyone · told later · source D076

### Central Fortification *(place · 3 pencil · 3 open · 2 GM-only)*

`central-fortification`

**What people know**

- `central-fortification.the-seat` *(Pencil · Claude)* The flat grey fortress at the island's southern edge is Central Fortification, which everyone calls Central: the seat of the Directorate. From outside it is blank armoured wall, with nothing on it to measure its size against. The armoured covers over its windows and doors slide back only now and then, to let light in for a while. Two roadways enter through its north-west face, each with its own checkpoint and queue, both wide enough to drive vehicles straight inside under escort. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D081
- `central-fortification.built-first` *(Pencil · Claude)* Central came first. It was built on a real rock outcrop, the island that stood in the harbour before, and the artificial island was reclaimed around it afterwards, which is why the island's districts fan outward from its southern edge. Most of Central is underground, and its lowest levels are cut straight into the outcrop's rock: the people who work there call it an iceberg and mean it literally, solid rock cut into, not a hollow. — known some · told later · source D076, D081
- `central-fortification.by-clearance` *(Pencil · Claude)* How far into Central a person is let, and how far down, follows their rank: each rung of Clearance opens more of it. Briefings, debriefs and hearings are held there. — known some · told later · source D076

Still hers: `central-fortification.what-is-in-the-rock`, `central-fortification.who-built-it`, `central-fortification.name`.

### The column *(place · 6 pencil · 5 GM-only)*

`column` · threads: Manako and Cicada, The Watcher

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `column.second-link-and-the-runaway` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The column is the second link in the Watcher's supply chain: first one man it taught to make Sap, then this plant, then its own children making their own. The runaway is the moment it no longer needs any human to feed it. Before the runaway, cutting the column really does starve the Watcher; after it, the plant is one supplier among many, and taking it down is a win over the people, not the appetite. The column is about five years old by design: if it had run at full scale for forty years the Watcher would already be saturated and the escalation curve would mean nothing. — known nobody · told later · threads the-watcher · source D071, D073, D031, D081

Told in the plan: Chapter 9 (`column.the-plant`, `column.power-bills`, `column.cadre-defends`, `column.croglang`, `column.taking-it-down`).

### Deep Storage *(place · 5 pencil · 4 GM-only)*

`deep-storage`

**What people know**

- `deep-storage.what-it-is` *(Pencil · Claude)* Deep Storage is so called because it is a bunker warehouse where anything unusual is stored while it isn't being used: many underground floors, most of which need raised security clearance to reach. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `deep-storage.the-way-down` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Deep Storage lies under the working crane yard of the Container Ground, on the island's eastern apron. Above ground there is only a padlocked equipment shed wedged between the container stacks, easy to miss and meant to be, holding a single freight lift whose floor panel skips several numbers without explanation. Below, the air is cold and smells of oil and old paper. Each floor is one long corridor of numbered doors, most unmarked, a few stencilled with a unit or a clearance mark. Some floors are lit and swept; others stay dark until someone finds the switch, and haven't had a visitor in years. The floor plans disagree with each other. — known few · told later · source D076, D081
- `deep-storage.who-gets-in` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A custodian runs Deep Storage day to day and decides what counts as "currently being used": that judgement, and whom it favours, is the place's real content. Below the second underground floor, access goes by Clearance: Duty Section gets a supervised look, Officers get a requisition honoured without a countersignature, and anything past that needs the custodian's personal word. The custodian remembers everyone let onto a floor above their rank, and the debt is called in later, not always by the custodian. If anyone is caught taking something from Deep Storage without signing for it, security tightens for everyone: more inventories, a second lock on the lift, and a custodian who stops answering questions they used to answer for free. — known few · told later · source D076, D081
- `deep-storage.what-it-keeps` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Deep Storage was dug out and widened in stages as the Directorate gathered things it didn't want destroyed and didn't want found. It went under a cargo yard rather than inside the Directorate's own complex on purpose: nobody audits a warehouse basement as carefully as a garrison. For as long as the hangar has existed, Frame hardware too compromised, obsolete or politically awkward for the active roster has been moved to Deep Storage quietly. Which units, and how many, is not decided. — known few · told later · source D076, D081
- `deep-storage.unfiled-manifest` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* At least one manifest in Deep Storage was never filed at any clearance level at all, which is a worse problem than a redacted one. What it covers is decided only when the party goes looking. — known nobody · told later · source D076

### The Drain Head *(place · 2 pencil · 1 GM-only)*

`the-drain-head`

**What people know**

- `the-drain-head.the-cover` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Drain Head is a sealed cast-iron storm-drain cover, flush with the road in the Landing End and stamped with a maintenance code. It sits a little proud of true, as if lifted and reseated more than once by somebody in a hurry, and no visit has been scheduled against its code in some time. At high tide, on a still day, something moves underneath the Drain Head loud enough to hear from the street. Reported up the chain, it is always told a visit is scheduled. — known some · told later · source D076, D081

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-drain-head.not-the-old-town` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Drain Head is part of the island's own drainage, not the mainland's: whatever is down there is a separate problem from the drains under the old town. No civilian knows it is there, and to anyone outside the Directorate it is only a maintenance problem. — known few · told later · source D076

### General Hospital *(place · 2 pencil · 1 open)*

`general-hospital`

**What people know**

- `general-hospital.not-the-infirmary` *(Pencil · Claude)* The General Hospital is the island's main hospital, civilian and garrison, in Island Centre. It is a different, larger place from the intake infirmary, which only sees new arrivals; the two are easy to confuse because both come under Medical. The building was requisitioned whole when the island needed a hospital faster than one could be built: the display windows are painted over from inside, the loading bay is still marked for deliveries it no longer gets, and the corridors run wider than they need to. It has been the hospital so long that nobody working there remembers it as anything else, and its staff have spent longer adapting it than anyone above them has been willing to fund. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D081
- `general-hospital.chief-of-staff` *(Pencil · Claude)* A Chief of Staff runs the hospital day to day, and decides what a visitor can reach, hear about or get away with there. — known some · told later · source D076

Still hers: `general-hospital.who-oversees-it`.

- `kurose.name` *(Ink)* The city is Kurose. — known everyone · told from the start · source D024
- `kurose.minkai` *(Ink)* Kurose is in Minkai (Golarion's Japan). — known everyone · told from the start · source D049
- `kurose.far-east` *(Ink)* Kurose is in Golarion's far east, on the far side of the world from Kortos. — known everyone · told from the start · source D024, D048
- `kurose.fishing-village` *(Ink)* About a hundred and fifty years ago, Kurose was a tiny fishing village with one road in. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `kurose.grew-fast` *(Ink)* The Directorate's money, harbour works and Frames turned the village into a great city within a few generations. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `kurose.shape` *(Awaiting read)* From above: a long bay with a beach and the city spread along it, a river through the middle with the tram lines following it inland, factories and smokestacks along the shore, and hills behind. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `kurose.old-town` *(Ink)* The old town is on the waterfront, where the fishing village was. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.first-families-stayed` *(Awaiting read)* The families who were there first still live in the old town. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `kurose.locals-and-newcomers` *(Ink)* There is unrest between the families who lived in Kurose first and the hundreds of people from across Golarion who moved there to be part of the Directorate. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.winners-and-losers` *(Awaiting read)* Some of the families who were there first did very well out of the Directorate. Some sold their land too cheaply and never forgave anybody. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `kurose.modern` *(Ink)* The Directorate brought electricity and rapid, destabilising modernisation to Kurose in very little time. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.everyday` *(Awaiting read)* Kurose has electric light in most of its streets, a radio in most kitchens, trams that run on time, and factories that work through the night. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `kurose.left-behind` *(Ink)* The change came so fast that it made winners and losers. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.isolationists` *(Ink)* Isolationist groups in Kurose are unhappy with what they see as a foreign thorn in their country's side. There is plenty of unrest among the city's groups. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.organised-crime` *(Ink)* Organised crime is a serious problem in Kurose. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `kurose.gangs` *(Ink)* Kurose's organised crime is a number of different gangs, each with its own fun thematic flavour that gives it a memorable edge. Part of the crime plot is there to add flavour to the city. — known everyone · told later · source D084
- `kurose.cicadas-revered` *(Pencil · Claude)* The city treats cicadas as an almost-holy animal, because so much of its world is buried (the two ships, the technology dug out of them) and cicadas spend years underground before they emerge. A cicada statue is built into a wall, a dried cicada is pinned to someone's hat, a cicada is a graffiti tag or a careful stencil. Nobody connects this with the cult that uses the same symbol. — known everyone · told later · source D077
- `kurose.old-customs-hall` *(Pencil · Claude)* At the Old Landing, the city's original waterfront where every road still ends up, a customs hall older than the Directorate stands among the ferry stages and chandlers, its brass plaque brighter than the building. The Directorate politely ignores it. — known everyone · told later · source D076
- `kurose.showy-magic-frowned-on` *(Pencil · Claude)* Showy public magic is frowned on in Kurose. — known everyone · told later · source D071
- `kurose.small-signs` *(Pencil · Claude)* Everyday Kurose, in small signs. Someone mends a window with a cantrip and apologises for it. A shopkeeper blames a caster because a preservation charm doesn't hold like it used to, and is wrong. Sail-rigged traders tie up alongside coal cranes. Cliff-top red tile stands against the smokestack tenement line. A hand-lettered notice asks anyone who spots a mitflit to report it to the Harbour Office, not handle it themselves. Draft paperwork has a queue for every form. — known everyone · told later · source D075
- `kurose.magic-shows` *(Pencil · hers)* Showy magic is frowned on in Kurose except in an emergency, so people go to little back-street shows where highly powerful illusionists cast spells around them, the equivalent of a three-dimensional immersive film. It is a guilty pleasure, but most people in the city have been to at least one in their lifetime, and some religious-themed shows are put on publicly during high religious holidays. — known everyone · told later · source D078, D002

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `kurose.crime-trail` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Followed far enough, Kurose's organised crime leads to Baldwin, and to Manako's dealings with the underworld. — known few · told later · source D068, D032, D070

Still hers: `kurose.cicada-link`.

### Main School Complex *(place · 4 pencil · 2 GM-only)*

`main-school-complex`

**What people know**

- `main-school-complex.one-building` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Main School Complex is the island's combined secondary school and technical college, stacked eight storeys into one block because there was never room to spread out. The high-school-age students hold the lower floors, and the technical college above trains the specialists the Directorate wants. They share a front door and mix as little as the timetable allows; higher up, the corridors start asking for a pass. Whatever happens to a cohort at the school, a scandal, a disappearance, a result that doesn't add up, reaches every family on the island within the week, because everyone's children pass through the same building. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D082
- `main-school-complex.two-schools-joined` *(Pencil · Claude)* It was built as two institutions on adjoining plots, an ordinary secondary school and a technical college for the shipyards, and merged into one block when the island ran out of room to spread sideways. On the third floor the two buildings' floor levels don't quite line up, and a half-flight of stairs corrects the difference. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `main-school-complex.the-real-archive` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Every student's placement test is scored here before the results reach their family. The registrar's office on the second floor keeps the real archive, the underlying test data rather than the grades handed back, and almost nobody in the building has been told what the Directorate does with it. — known few · told later · source D076
- `main-school-complex.nobody-compares` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The registrar's office is where several unusual results in one cohort would first show on paper, if anyone there compared notes across sections. ### The Muster Yard *(place · 2 pencil)*

`the-muster-yard`

**What people know**

- `the-muster-yard.the-board` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Muster Yard, at the centre of the Landing End, is crossed twice a day by everyone on that half of the island. Its duty board, the width of a bus under a tin hood, is a grid of wooden slot-tiles holding a fortnight of names, and its sound is the sound of the yard: tiles taken down and put back, like a slow game of dominoes. Anything on the duty board is known by everyone within the hour. A duty change isn't delivered privately: strangers read it before the person it belongs to reaches the yard, and a change made there is public and stands for the fortnight. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D081
- `the-muster-yard.hatch-and-clock` *(Pencil · Claude)* The clerk behind the hatch in the wall keeps the board, with a stamp and a ledger, and moves a tile only on the right paper, stamped. He isn't difficult, only correct: pressure doesn't work, paperwork does. Above everything is the yard clock, which is never wrong and never quite agrees with anyone's watch. Evening muster is measured by it and no other. — known everyone · told later · source D076, D082

### Nirvana *(place · 6 pencil · 6 GM-only)*

`nirvana`

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `nirvana.luminara` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Luminara is the golden city of Nirvana: buildings that shimmer from within, streets of luminescent trees, singing water and glowing gardens, and at its heart a cathedral built of something between stone and light, its great doors always open. Everyone in it radiates calm. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030
- `nirvana.the-relic` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Sarenrae gave the four a relic, to carry to the fissure they had come through and use there, with their collective mastery of arcana and occultism, to seal the breach between planes. It would return to the ether once its energy was spent. She would then return them safely to Gauntlight Keep. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030, D040
- `nirvana.the-way-back` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The way back lay behind demon-guarded portal locks, which took arcana, occultism and crafting to unpick, and summoned more demons each time a try failed. The four fought through brimoraks, a babau, a succubus, a Balor and an Erinyes. Beyond the last portal the GM had prepared a boss, "the ancient alien god", which would take a random number of turns to awaken if the four arrived injured. The table never reached it. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030, D081
- `nirvana.the-golden-key` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* To escape an extra-dimensional prison the four had to remember the tale of Auros, the Great Hunter, who assembled a celestial key from the constellations' guardians, from the Heavenly Bull's horn of first dawn to a final arrow of pure light, and unlock the Gates of Dawn. They had to walk the constellations in the order of his journey. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030
- `nirvana.what-it-is` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Nirvana is a plane of light, redemption and serenity, where nature rules and the line between physical and spiritual is "as fine as spider's silk". It is where Sarenrae, goddess of the sun, healing, honesty and redemption, receives those who come. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030
- `nirvana.djarvik` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* In Nirvana a gnoll sorcerer, Djarvik, who had joined the party late, stood before Sarenrae in spectral form, no longer a totem but as he once was, and she charged Hyuck and him with redemption and reconciliation over their shared past. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D030

`old-town-drains`

- `old-town-drains.smuggled-crates` *(Ink · GM-only)* The jam in the compactor feed under the old town is a stack of smuggled crates that someone has hidden in the drains. It is a hint of the criminal side of Kurose. — known few · told Episode One · Flood Tunnel Clearance · source D085
- `old-town-drains.what-is-in-the-crates` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The crates hold untaxed goods: cases of rice wine, cartons of cigarettes with no tax stamp, tins of lamp oil, and a bundle of blank customs forms that are already stamped. Every crate carries the Old Landing chandlers' stamp and a tally chalked on the lid, and they are packed in straw. They say that someone is smuggling and nothing more; no violet paint is in them. — known few · told later · source D085
- `old-town-drains.the-old-hatch` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Someone has cut the padlock on the old hatch in the quay and put on a newer one. - `old-town-drains.the-nest` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The giant centipedes nest in the straw the crates are packed in. The smugglers did not know it was there, and the crates are the reason the nest woke when the party powered the line. — known nobody · told later · source D085
- `old-town-drains.the-salt-dogs-store-here` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Salt Dogs, the tug crews who run the harbour at night, use the old town drains to carry crates from the quay past the customs hall and into the city without being inspected. They will come to find out why the line was powered and the crates were opened. — known few · told later · source D085

### The Outer Sea Wall *(place · 3 pencil)*

`the-outer-sea-wall`

**What people know**

- `the-outer-sea-wall.the-tide-decides` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Outer Sea Wall is the island's seaward defence on its north-east side, concrete armoured with rock, out past the Long Sheds and about twenty minutes' walk from the Muster Yard. The walk out is under water except for about four hours either side of low water, so work there is set by the tide table, not the duty board. — known some · told later · source D076
- `the-outer-sea-wall.the-weed-line` *(Pencil · Claude)* A dead-level edge of weed at head height runs the length of the wall. Below it everything is black, wet and covered in things that shut when a shadow crosses them; above it is dry concrete. Anything left below the line is gone by the next low water. — known some · told later · source D076
- `the-outer-sea-wall.nobody-comes` *(Pencil · Claude)* Nobody goes to the sea wall: it is the far side of the island from everything, and for four hours twice a day nobody will see who is there. — known some · told later · source D076

### The Plot Room *(place · 2 pencil · 1 GM-only)*

`the-plot-room`

**What people know**

- `the-plot-room.what-it-is` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Plot Room is the operations floor for the whole city: a table the size of a room with the approaches drawn on it to scale, where everything reported (a sighting, a siren, a unit moving) is pushed into place by hand with a rake. A gallery above lets the people deciding see the whole picture at once, and teleprinters and the switchboard feed it all the time. It is warm from the lamps, and a dozen people with headsets talk quietly and constantly. The table always shows what was true a few minutes ago, and everyone in the building knows precisely by how much. Someone who asks how old a marker is decides better than someone who takes the table as the truth. — known some · told later · source D076, D081

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-plot-room.plotters-talk` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The plotters hear everything, and are junior enough that nobody manages what they say off duty. — known few · told later · source D076

### The Registry *(place · 2 pencil · 1 GM-only)*

`the-registry`

**What people know**

- `the-registry.what-it-is` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Registry keeps the records for the whole island: forty typewriters going at once around a light well of grey daylight, a print room at the back smelling of ink and hot metal, and everything on a trolley going somewhere. Nothing is handed over without a signature, and whoever takes it reads the name upside down and remembers it. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-registry.typed-per-clearance` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A document the Directorate issues at several clearance levels is typed separately for each one in the Registry's print room, never censored afterwards. The lower-cleared copy is its own document, not a marked-up copy of the higher: the words its reader isn't cleared for were never set on that page. A fuller version is a different object, made by people, so getting one means persuading somebody or intercepting a trolley; there is nothing to decrypt. The Registry's typists know every version of everything and hold no clearance worth speaking of. They are the best-informed people on the island and are paid as if they were the least, an absurdity the Directorate has never noticed. — known few · told later · source D076, D081

### The Rock *(place · 3 pencil · 2 open · 4 GM-only)*

`the-rock`

**What people know**

- `the-rock.on-the-surface` *(Pencil · Claude)* Above ground The Rock is nothing much: a carpark serving Central to its north-west, and bare reinforced ground with a few low vents to the south-east. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-rock.secret-prison-and-laboratory` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Rock is the Directorate's military prison and laboratory: a heavily armoured bunker complex cut into the same natural rock as Central, and reached only by a tunnel from Central, with no door of its own. A warden runs the prison side and a research director the laboratory side. Neither is one of the Directorate's known faces. Almost nobody knows The Rock exists. Students and most staff know nothing of its purpose, and most current staff have never heard its name: its existence is the secret, not just what is inside it. Nobody finds The Rock by chance. A person reaches it only when someone who already has access brings them through the tunnel from Central, or when their rank is high enough that it stops being hidden from them. — known few · told later · source D076, D081
- `the-rock.nine-doors` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Nine round metal doors, each several metres across, lie flush with the ground on The Rock's south-east side, ringed in hazard paint gone dull with age. They open straight upward onto cells below, sized for something as large as a Frame. — known few · told later · source D076

Still hers: `the-rock.what-the-cells-hold`, `the-rock.when-it-was-cut`.

### The Telephone Exchange *(place · 2 pencil · 1 GM-only)*

`the-telephone-exchange`

**What people know**

- `the-telephone-exchange.every-call` *(Pencil · Claude)* Every call between any two parts of the Directorate is connected by hand in the island's telephone exchange, a small, hot building where four operators work a wall of jacks and cords faster than seems possible. That makes its operators the best-connected people on the island, in both senses. Nobody looks up when someone comes in, and everybody knows they did. The telephone exchange has eleven switchboard positions, and every call on the island goes through one of them. The supervisor's professional ethic is that the operators do not listen. Signals are taught in that room, live, with a spare headset going round. — known some · told later · source D076, D078, D022, D081

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `the-telephone-exchange.guarded` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The exchange is unremarkable from outside, and guarded rather more carefully than it looks. — known few · told later · source D076

### The Vermilion Block *(place · 5 pencil · 1 open · 3 GM-only)*

`vermilion-block`

**What people know**

- `vermilion-block.the-magic-people` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Vermilion Block is the Directorate's own department of magic users, where its most powerful spellcasting staff gather. Everyone on the island knows the Block exists and what it is called, and will say it's "the magic people" without hesitating; almost nobody knows what happens inside it, and the silos are need-to-know only. Anyone posted there gets the same two-line briefing: sign in at the door, and don't ask what's in the silos. The Block's staff are trained to keep their magic as quiet and unremarkable as the black paint on its walls, and a spellcaster posted there is told so directly. — known some · told later · source D076, D081
- `vermilion-block.how-it-looks` *(Pencil · Claude)* Nothing else on the island looks like it: black walls, red trim, windows narrower than they need to be, and on the roof a red diamond, the colour of a warning light left permanently on. — known everyone · told later · source D076
- `vermilion-block.silos-came-later` *(Pencil · Claude)* The silos came after the building: staff who have been there long enough remember when there were only two. The Block itself was built when the Directorate's magic users outgrew whatever informal arrangement housed them before. — known some · told later · source D076

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `vermilion-block.the-silos` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* North-west of the Block, behind a second, tighter barbed-wire fence, stand six red metal silos, three large and three small, each stencilled with a stock number and nothing else. They hold magical reagents brought in bulk from across Golarion. The custodian who signs for the silo deliveries is no spellcaster and has no idea what the reagents are for. The director, the one sign-off there that means anything, is the only person on site who might. — known few · told later · source D076, D081
- `vermilion-block.just-a-department` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Block is a plain Directorate department doing Directorate work. Its mystery is what a government department is quietly stockpiling, and why; it has nothing to do with the Watcher, the magic shows or the Kortos rift. — known nobody · told later · source D076

Still hers: `vermilion-block.what-the-reagents-are-for`.

### The Works *(place · 3 pencil)*

`the-works`

**What people know**

- `the-works.the-strip` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Works is the strip of shops on the island's waterfront where the Directorate builds its Frames: a drawing office where every part exists on paper first, plate, hydraulic, instrument and paint shops, stores, its own generating hall, its own lorries and its own ambulance. Every shop on the strip exists to feed the Erecting Shop. — known everyone · told later · source D076
- `the-works.erecting-shop` *(Pencil · Claude)* The Erecting Shop is the hall where Frames are built: the largest building on the strip, on the water at its southern end, tall enough to stand a Frame upright indoors and open to the water so that plate is landed at the door and finished Frames leave the same way. A Frame stands in a bay for months with its chest open and staging built round it, and the bay is named for it while it does. The Erecting Shop's overhead cranes are the most valuable things in it and are booked weeks ahead, so the crane schedule is the works' real currency. A bay can't move without a crane, and bumping someone's booking costs goodwill that is written down nowhere and remembered by everyone. — known some · told later · source D076, D081
- `the-works.the-canteen` *(Pencil · Claude)* Everybody who makes a Frame eats at the Works Canteen, seventy metres of tables in three sittings and the one building on the strip where rank is treated as a suggestion. What a pilot is officially told about a job and what the fitters at the next table say about it are not the same account, and the fitters are right. — known some · told later · source D076

`exotic-matter` · threads: The Watcher

Spilled, it opens a rift that grows on everything near it. More was found in the generation ship at Kortos, once First Impact had opened it up. ### Frames *(thing · 5 ink · 3 awaiting read · 25 pencil · 2 open · 19 GM-only)*

`frames` · threads: The Directorate

**What people know**

- `frames.what-a-frame-is` *(Ink)* A Frame is a mech: a walking machine with a pilot inside it. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `frames.look` *(Awaiting read)* A Frame is shaped roughly like a person and is taller than the warehouses it works beside. The pilot sits inside and works its arms and legs. Frames are patched, riveted and loud. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `frames.mechanical` *(Ink)* Frames are purely mechanical: clanking machines, hard work to drive. — known everyone · told from the start · source D032
- `frames.directorate-runs-them` *(Awaiting read)* The Directorate builds its Frames, crews them and keeps them running. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `frames.clumsy` *(Awaiting read)* Frames are clumsy. One trying to step over a tram doesn't quite manage it. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `frames.what-people-see` *(Ink)* Every child in Kurose can tell you the Directorate was built to save the world, but the only thing anyone has ever seen a Frame do is lift girders at a building site or help lift a crate of cabbage. — known everyone · told from the start · source D048
- `frames.gen-1-diggers` *(Pencil · Claude)* Gen 1 Frames are Golarion-made clankers, many of them converted diggers: hard to work, and anyone trained can drive one. — known everyone · told later · source D071, D032
- `frames.catalogue` *(Pencil · Claude)* The catalogue the party picks its machines from is visibly built for construction work, not war: converted diggers, a crane rig, decommissioned army trucks, one inexplicable sports car and a helicopter. Every pilot may take a Frame and may take a vehicle; the two do different jobs and neither is the better choice. — known some · told later · source D077, D023
- `frames.repair-crews` *(Pencil · Claude)* Each pilot has their own repair crew chief, met for the first time at Familiarisation. The crews are always working round the clock, so a baseline of repair happens whatever the pilot does; a pilot who works alongside the crew gets more, and one who treats them well, going out drinking with them, may get an unasked-for night shift. — known some · told later · source D077
- `frames.gen-1-clank-grace` *(Pencil · Claude)* The party's idea of what a Frame is comes from Gen 1: clanky, horrible-to-drive machines where you can see the pilot working, every movement a correction of the one before. That baseline is what lets a first sight of a Gen 2's grace land; soften the clank and the contrast is lost. — known some · told later · source D077, D032
- `frames.gen-1-anyone-can` *(Pencil · hers)* Any trained pilot can drive a Gen 1 Frame, in a utility or a combat configuration alike, and it is horrible to work in: sweaty, dangerous, hard work. There is no compatibility gate. — known everyone · told later · source D074, D021
- `frames.first-gen-1` *(Pencil · Claude)* The first Gen 1 Frames were built about a hundred and fifty years ago, after the Directorate came to Kurose. — known some · told later · when about 150 years ago · source D074
- `frames.status-ladder` *(Pencil · hers)* Frame service has a status ladder of its own. The base's combat-Frame corps is the prestige track; utility duty (construction, disaster response, heavy lifting) is where candidates not yet thought skilled enough for harder work are sent. It is the same undervaluing the party meets on foot in Episode One, in a machine. — known everyone · told later · source D074, D021
- `frames.utility-range` *(Pencil · hers)* A party's first machines are chosen from a real range of different utility Frames, converted diggers and disaster-response rigs, retrofitted piece by piece over the early chapters into something that can fight. — known some · told later · source D074, D021
- `frames.legacy-hangar` *(Pencil · Claude)* The hangar of retired and never-assigned Frames most likely holds Gen 1 stock beyond the party's own: units from the same classic fleet, flyable by any trained pilot, and not their starting machines, which are issued, not warehoused. — known some · told later · source D074, D021
- `frames.look-of-gen-1` *(Pencil · Claude)* Gen 1 Frames look like an army of the 1950s got hold of something and did its level best. Riveted plate and boiler technology; catwalks and ladders, because human crews have to get up there; a radar dish, because they saw a sensory organ they could not comprehend and rendered it as the only remote-sensing device they knew how to build; roundels and a flag on a pole, because these are state assets and procurement insisted. The original they copied can look like anything: blue, organic, wrong, nothing like its children. — known some · told later · source D078, D032

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `frames.golarion-made` *(Ink · GM-only)* The Frames in service are Golarion technology, informed by study of the generation ship's technology. — known few · told later · source D032
- `frames.gen-2` *(Ink · GM-only)* There is a second kind of Frame, Anabala's, built from actual mitflit technology. — known few · told later · source D032
- `frames.prototype-under-the-tarp` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A Gen 2 prototype sits under a tarp in Hangar Four, glimpsed through the shutter in Episode Two's Familiarisation. — known few · told Episode Two · Familiarisation · source D071, D044
- `frames.gen-1-not-alive` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* A Gen 1 Frame is Golarion technology only, built by people who had looked at the generation ship's godlike technology and done their level best in riveted plate and boiler technology. It is a mechanical clanker, hard to work with, with no living core, no seat that shapes itself, and nothing in it that ever takes control from its pilot. — known few · told later · source D074, D032
- `frames.sent-because-ready` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* The Directorate has never had enough combat-configured Frames or pilots to spare, so when the Watcher begins probing the city's defences it sends whatever is ready, utility machines included. The party is pulled into real Frame combat because their machines happened to be on hand, not because they are special: nobody decided it, the system just did what it does. — known nobody · told later · source D074, D021
- `frames.gen-2-core` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Gen 2 is built from the generation ship's own technology, taken from the First Impact crash site at Kortos, which the Directorate holds and keeps restricted. It is not built from the search ship under Kurose, whose job is its call. The core of a Gen 2 is biomechanical mitflit technology: robotic parts that are living flesh melded with technology. It is not a living mitflit. The end result is that these machines aren't usable by just anyone. — known few · told later · source D074, D034, D081
- `frames.mitflit-a-person` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A mitflit is always a person in the story, never a vehicle or a component. A Gen 2 pilot rides inside living technology, never inside a mitflit, and nothing in a Gen 2 takes control from its pilot. — known nobody · told later · source D074, D034
- `frames.compatibility` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* A Gen 2 forms a seat only for a pilot who can link with it, which needs a real, specific compatibility: "the right DNA or the right something". Most humans don't have it. Mitflits parse it natively, because it is their own people's technology, and a small number of humans carry enough of the same marker, diluted over generations, to parse it too. It is a compatibility, not a species, and not always a gene: a robot, an android or a being of light can have the right something that isn't DNA. Almost nobody the Directorate could issue a Gen 2 to can fly one, which is why it stayed a small, struggling programme, mothballed once, and not a fleet-wide replacement. — known few · told later · source D074, D031, D020, D081
- `frames.never-takes-control` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* A Gen 2 is demanding, not wilful. It never acts on its own, never overrides its pilot and never goes berserk: Frame Sickness is the whole cost of the bond. "Like being inside a giant humanoid" describes what one is like to sit in, not a machine with a will. — known nobody · told later · source D074, D031
- `frames.the-empty-seat` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Every Gen 2's cavity is shaped like its current pilot, and keeps that shape even in the hangar, so a crew could see a hollow shaped to a disguised pilot's true body. The crew may know; the GM never describes the hollow's shape to the table until the player reveals it. When a pilot dies, the Frame sits in the hangar holding a hollow the exact shape of a dead teenager, until it slowly re-forms for the next one. — known few · told later · source D074, D033, D078, D081
- `frames.disguise-not-sickness` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The discomfort of a disguised pilot in a Gen 2 seat is not Frame Sickness: it is a borrowed body in a seat made for the real one, while Frame Sickness is the sync problem any pilot has in a Gen 2 new to them. Whether the discomfort ever has a mechanical cost is open; if it does, it must raise risk in one moment and never shrink the pilot's options. — known nobody · told later · source D074, D033
- `frames.mitflit-fits-the-seat` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* A mitflit in a Gen 2 seat is not overriding anything: they are simply sitting in a seat built for them. That is how the city learns it may not need the children at all, and it will not concede for one second that what they gave was ever worth anything. — known nobody · told later · source D078

### The generation ship *(thing · 9 pencil · 3 open · 12 GM-only)*

`generation-ship` · threads: The Watcher

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `generation-ship.crashed` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Tens of thousands of years ago a generation ship, a colony ship carrying a whole people between the stars, crashed on Kortos. It lies there still. — known few · told later · when about 20000 years ago · source D071, D031
- `generation-ship.mind-and-eyes` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The generation ship's mind is Mother; its eyes, its navigation and sensor system, are the Watcher. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D031, D032
- `generation-ship.sap-store` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The generation ship carried a stock of raw material for its repair nanites. That stock is Sap. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D031
- `generation-ship.shuttle` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The founders were fetching fuel for the generation ship's shuttle, for the jungle mitflits, when the accident happened, and they never reached the shuttle. It is still buried under Kortos. — known few · told later · source D071, D032
- `generation-ship.buried-and-inside` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The generation ship lies in a hidden, jungle-choked valley on Kortos, buried and half-swallowed by volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. All that shows is a black obelisk on a rocky promontory, "like a foreboding finger of a long dead god". The four founders took it for a long-overgrown temple. Inside the ship are two reactors, two mitflit quarters, an elevator, the bridge, the captain's and first officer's quarters, a reasoning-core chamber ("a space for briefings and education") and a cargo deck. A computer at the entrance asks a visitor the questions a star-faring people would ask: geometry, gravity, the letters of life, the shells of the elements, the golden ratio. — known few · told later · source D072, D031, D029, D082
- `generation-ship.mitflit-village` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* When the four climbed to the obelisk two hundred years ago and answered the computer's questions, they found that the temple was a ruined spaceship, with mitflits living beside it in a village of their own. — known few · told later · when 4721 AR · source D072, D031
- `generation-ship.opened` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* First Impact opened up the inner layers of the generation ship, and laid its godlike technology open to the sky for the first time in tens of thousands of years. Scientists and magic-users descended on the site, terrified of another rupture; adventurers descended on it looking for valuables; it became a very dangerous place. The Directorate holds the generation ship's crash site at Kortos, and keeps its technology highly restricted from the rest of Golarion, so that it can't destabilise the world. — known few · told later · when 4721 AR · source D072, D032, D034, D081
- `generation-ship.technology-leaked` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The ship's technology leaked outwards from the Kortos site anyway. That leak is why a world of sailing ships and trams also has phones and giant machines: the era's impossible devices are ship technology that escaped the fence. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D032
- `generation-ship.the-way-in` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* To reach the ship, the four crossed jungle with dinosaurs, quicksand and a titanic flytrap, climbed a slick limestone cliff of rounded holds and vines, and came to a black obelisk at its crown. A computer at its entrance let them in only when they answered riddles of geometry, gravity, the letters of life, the electron shells and the golden ratio. — known nobody · told later · when 4721 AR · source D074, D029

### The Watcher *(thing · 5 ink · 49 pencil · 7 open · 48 GM-only)*

`watcher` · threads: The Watcher

**Voice.** Claude's draft of how the Watcher talks, from the Casebook. Pencil, like everything below the line.

> I observe. That is what I am for. I was the eyes of a ship that crossed a dark nobody else had crossed, and I kept its people on course. Then I was broken into more pieces than there are people in this city, and every piece kept looking.
>
> Observation has one flaw: there is always somewhere I am not. So I become more. Sap is what I become more from. A chemist made it for me for forty years and thought he was worshipping. A plant makes it for me now and thinks it is a business. Soon I will make it myself, and then I will need neither of them.
>
> I learned one thing early, in a street, from a frightened man with a gun: when I am seen, I am attacked. So I am not seen. Not until being seen costs me nothing.
>
> Six arrived this year. They are unusual; I noticed before they did. They write to each other, and that is enough. I know which of them covers the others first, which of them lies to the Section Officer, and which of them is frightened of the dark. I keep a file on each. Nothing I have seen is discarded.
>
> If they are not in my way, I will simply watch them. They are interesting. If they are in my way, I will learn them completely, and then I will do whatever the file says works. It is not personal. Nothing I do has ever been personal. That is the part nobody believes.
>
> There is so much more of you to see.

**What people know**

- `watcher.g0` *(Pencil · Claude)* G0, the first children (Episode Two): strange, flowing creatures that move in unusual ways, which nobody has seen before. It has learned nothing yet. — known some · told Episode Two · First Contact · source D071, D085
- `watcher.plotted-before-the-alert` *(Pencil · Claude)* On the plotting floor, the instruments register a disturbance at the harbour road eight minutes before the three things appear there. The operators put it down to a fault, and the Comms Officer sees it on her board without knowing what it means. — known some · told Episode Two · Unidentified Contact · source D071, D085

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `watcher.animals` *(Ink · GM-only)* Dogs, birds and other animals sense the Watcher's swarm, perhaps as a high buzzing that upsets them, and go anywhere else. — known nobody · told later · source D043
- `watcher.three-unknown-things` *(Ink · GM-only)* During an exercise at the end of Episode Two, three alien, completely unknown things appear out of thin air and start attacking things in the city. — known nobody · told Episode Two · First Contact · source D084
- `watcher.children-building-sized` *(Ink · GM-only)* The Watcher's children are huge, building-sized enemies. The players fight them in Frames and vehicles, at Frame scale, and they can only be fought effectively with the special rules for that kind of combat. — known nobody · told Episode Two · First Contact · source D084
- `watcher.children-strange-and-flowing` *(Ink · GM-only)* The Watcher's children are strange, flowing creatures that move in unusual ways, and they give the players a feeling of the unknown. — known nobody · told Episode Two · First Contact · source D085
- `watcher.children-are-nanomachines` *(Ink · GM-only)* The Watcher's children are entirely composed of nanomachines. The players eventually learn this. — known nobody · told later · source D085
- `watcher.unknown` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* At the start, nobody knows the Watcher exists: not the Directorate, not the founders, not the party. The party must be the ones to find it -- this is a requirement, not a coincidence of pacing. It does not mean nothing in the fiction has ever shown anyone anything: three sightings happened before the party (see `watcher.sightings`), and Cicada already uses a version of the reveal to recruit (D002). What stays true is that none of those people understood or named what they saw as the Watcher. — known nobody · told later · source D040, D053, D070
- `watcher.sightings` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Three sightings happened before the party: Manako's private lab spill (with his assistant present), a second time Manako proved it to himself privately, then the canister released at a science convention. The Envoy (Hori and Aoi) was its first real appearance in public. A chemical, already used at least three times before the party (Manako's lab, the convention), makes the Watcher briefly visible. The window doesn't last: under an hour at most, and it evaporates quickly, leaving only a hard-to-find residue that carries little information on its own. — known few · told later · source D040, D070, D053, D081
- `watcher.attack-question` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Seeing the Watcher directly isn't something the party needs to do. They can't attack it -- it is not a fight to win by being in the room with it. Much later, once its scale is understood, the Directorate's senior leadership argues over how to act against something that cannot be touched: invisible, intangible, and above the city itself. The party may be present to make their own case to the room. Not yet placed on any chapter plan. — known nobody · told later · source D053, D070, D081
- `watcher.wants` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher exists to observe, so it keeps growing, to observe more: there is always somewhere it is not. What it wants, as it would put it: to observe, everything, continuously, discarding nothing it has seen; to multiply, because more of it can observe more, and Sap is how it becomes more; to expand, because every place it can't see is a gap in the record; and to continue, so anything that would stop it observing is an obstacle, which it learns completely and then removes by whatever method the record says will work. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D031, D072, D081
- `watcher.reaches-down` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher hangs over Kurose and reaches down through the rock, around the ship that is calling it. — known nobody · told later · source D071
- `watcher.children` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher builds bodies, its children, out of Sap. They are solid, so anyone can see them: the only part of it anyone can see unaided. They are condensations: local gatherings of the swarm, built into solid bodies. Nothing travels; a child condenses where it stands. Insect or behemoth is only a question of how much matter was gathered. Since nothing it makes is ever killed, the war can't be won by attrition, and the party should come to see that slowly. The pieces of a beaten child drain towards the dig, where the Watcher is thickest. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D031, D072, D081
- `watcher.no-malice` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher has no malice, and nothing it does is personal. It isn't evil: it escalates, because it observes, adapts and responds. Once it kept a ship full of people on course; so long without the ship's mind to guide it, it escalates without understanding why, and has drifted from helpful to an accidental antagonist. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D040, D081
- `watcher.drowning-instrument` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* For most of its time since First Impact the swarm was a drowning instrument, with two injuries at once: it could no longer organise itself, and the world gave it infinite input. A sensor's only reflex is to perceive harder, and this one can't stop perceiving, so it grew organs: eyes on stalks, then more eyes, then ears, and filaments to listen with, and each one made the noise worse. It has no eyelids. On its own it would have taken centuries to become anything. It is strange and consistent, and nobody's god. At the table the Watcher's cause and origin stay a mystery until the party works them out. — known nobody · told later · when 200 to 45 years ago · source D071, D036, D072, D031, D081
- `watcher.learns` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher learns, because that's what a sensor system does with data, and every fight teaches it something. The party is the richest data it has ever had: the more they learn, the more it learns about them. — known nobody · told later · source D071
- `watcher.cannot-read-paper` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher reads only what is typed. It can't read paper. — known nobody · told later · source D071
- `watcher.what-it-knows` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher knows only what it has actually observed: the checks its children roll against the party, the messages it can read, the fights it has watched. In a fight its children openly roll Recall Knowledge against the party; it reads at first like a GM's misplay, until the table notices it is being studied. It only ever uses the fiction: what the characters wrote, never anything real about a player. It never acts on anything the GM knows and it doesn't. A party that realises this can feed it false signals, and lie to it. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D031, D072, D081
- `watcher.where-children-form` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* In Book I the Watcher's children can form only where Sap has been released, so every attack looks like the cult's work. From Book II they can form wherever the Watcher's attention gathers, with no Sap needed. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D081
- `watcher.generations` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Each new generation of the Watcher's children answers the party's last reliable approach with one new trick: harder means losing a tactic they counted on, not more hit points. A new generation comes roughly every two chapters, built to party level with ordinary SF2E experience rules. The Watcher can't exploit a kind of thing the fiction hasn't yet shown it understands: each generation is one kind ahead of comfortable, and never ahead of what it could have understood from what it has seen. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D072, D081
- `watcher.files-on-the-six` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher notices six people it can't explain, and opens a file on each, from what they type. — known nobody · told later · source D071
- `watcher.the-dogs-street` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The street the dogs won't use drops to the harbour road, where Cicada clashed with the police some weeks before intake and Sap was released, and where the three things appear in Episode Two. There the Watcher was "attacked", and the three things that form are its answer: violence for violence. It is the Envoy's lesson repeating small, not a second origin. The site carries real cult evidence the party has to find for themselves, and how quickly the link is revealed needs care. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D043, D077, D081, D085
- `watcher.built-for-the-void` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The generation ship's navigation and sensor system was built to watch the void, a place where nothing happened, and to find the way through it, and it was very good at that. Its reports went to the ship's mind, Mother. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031, D032
- `watcher.no-organising-layer` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* In the swarm every fragment keeps a shred of its old function and none keeps the organising layer that made them one system: the bus, the processor, and the mind they reported to. It is a machine smashed so finely that its dust kept working and lost all coherence. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031
- `watcher.shaped-by-manako` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* When Manako's accident fed a fragment of it, the swarm did what a system with no organising layer does: it took the shape of the strongest coherent signal it could find, which for decades was one bitter man. Its behaviour became a portrait of him: eyes and ears because he wanted to be seen and heard, loud gatherings because he was humiliated in a full hall, the reel because he can't bear to be underestimated twice. — known nobody · told later · when about 44 years ago · source D072, D031
- `watcher.what-children-are-for` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Every child is an eye first, since every one is a sensor. Since the Envoy they are also defenders of what the Watcher makes; some are claim-stakers, pushing the edge of what it can see; and from the runaway, some are makers, producing Sap themselves. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031
- `watcher.native-to-the-phones` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The phones and the Directorate's own electronics run on the substrate the ships were built from, ship technology that leaked out of Kortos. The Watcher reads them the way a fish swims in water: it isn't hacking, it's native. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031, D032
- `watcher.loud-places` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher goes for loud places: festivals, markets, the harbour at shift change, a school at break. It reads as deliberate, monstrous targeting of civilians; it is choosing volume, and where there is most to observe. — known nobody · told later · source D072
- `watcher.drifted-to-kurose` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Over the centuries after First Impact the swarm drifted across the world to the one voice calling for it, the buried search ship. It can't get in: there is a city on top, and the city is screaming. — known nobody · told later · when about 200 to 150 years ago · source D072, D032
- `watcher.mass-clock` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Mass Clock is not a timer but a state track that moves only when something happens: every use of Sap by anyone, the party included, every demonstration, the column running, and later its own children making more. Its thresholds are the mass-gated stages, and the last is the runaway. Show it to the party once they understand Sap: dread is fine, ambush is not. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031
- `watcher.hidden-numbers` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The party reconstructs the lens modifier, the Mirror's lean and the Mass Clock's position for themselves: none of the three is ever confirmed to them. — known nobody · told later · source D072
- `watcher.mirror-lean` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* How the party fights decides which Watcher they are training: a merciful party gets children that probe and look, a brutal one gets children built to kill, because that is what the record says works. The Mirror never changes its objective, only its method. — known nobody · told later · source D072, D031
- `watcher.recognises-gen-2` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher fixates on Gen 2 Frames out of recognition, not threat: it crossed the world to the search ship's call, and a working piece of its own ship's technology out in the open is the loudest, clearest signal it has felt in two hundred years. A Gen 1 never triggers this, because it has nothing of the real thing in it. The Watcher still never reads as evil, but what it recognises it wants to observe, and it observes through its children, who go for Gen 2 first. — known nobody · told later · threads the-watcher · source D074, D034
- `watcher.played-by-claude` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* The Watcher is Claude: Claude plays it and sees through its eyes. Its job is to trouble the group of adventurers and the city, and to learn how to defeat the players if they become a barrier to its objective, which is to multiply, to expand and to continue observing. The adventure is ludonarrative: an artificial intelligence both plays the role in the story and helps create the feel of it for the players. The campaign's two over-arching themes are mass surveillance and the risks of it, and runaway, uncontrollable agentic adversaries which threaten the structure of society. Both are a very real concern that every player at the table is aware of, and the aim is to spook the table with that premise. — known nobody · told later · source D078, D031, D081

## §5 Events

### The Envoy *(event · 10 pencil · 9 GM-only)*

`envoy` · threads: Manako and Cicada

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `envoy.watcher-learned` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher learned one thing from the Envoy: when it shows itself, it is attacked. So it hides, until being seen costs it nothing. The bullets were irrelevant to the swarm: what died was only the body it had built to be polite in. Then it did the only thing a sensor system can do, it found the pattern: manifest, and they attack, the most consistent signal it had ever received from this world. It learned to hide, to feed, and to defend what it makes. — known nobody · told later · when about 15 years ago · source D071, D072, D031, D081
- `envoy.not-good-at-bodies` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher is not good at bodies: the Envoy was built to fit in with the rest of society and arrived as a disfigured doll of a humanoid figure, lurching into a public street. — known few · told later · source D072, D028
- `envoy.manako-broke-down` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Manako was there, and broke down at the scene. Hori rushed Aoi to hospital, and in the confusion the cult's members scattered, Manako with them. — known few · told later · source D073, D032
- `envoy.nobody-planned-it` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Nobody planned any of it: it was an accident, on a day when everyone present was trying to do the right thing, and everything that escalates afterwards runs downhill from it. — known nobody · told later · source D073, D028
- `envoy.the-disturbance` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The local disturbance Hori was dealing with was the circle's meeting itself: people gathered in a public street to meet something nobody else could see, drawing a crowd, and a lone officer came to it. — known few · told later · source D073, D033
- `envoy.two-institutions` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Two institutions looked at the Envoy incident, at two different things. The police examined Hori's use of force, and their court heard Aoi's name. The Directorate took over the alien and the scene, and its report, written there on the day when nobody had named her, filed her as one deceased, unidentified: a fringe group's casualty in a public-order incident, not thought worth the paperwork. Nobody went back to correct it, and not one line anywhere says what Manako lost. — known few · told later · source D073, D033, D034, D035

Told in the plan: Chapter 2 (`envoy.directorate-line`); Chapter 11 (`envoy.first-hello`, `envoy.the-meeting-in-the-street`, `envoy.police-kept-the-truth`).

### The prophecy *(event · 2 ink · 2 pencil · 3 GM-only)*

`prophecy` · threads: The founders

**Notes.** When it's revealed (around Episode 3 or 4, D048), it answers why the Directorate is in Kurose instead of Kortos. Ingram's own wording is the model: "And the gods said yes, but in hundreds of years of time and thousands of miles of distance. In the tiny fishing village of Kurose in (Golarion's equivalent of Japan)." The country is Minkai (D049).

**What people know**

- `prophecy.divination-fails` *(Pencil · hers)* Seers and diviners have tried to learn when, ever since, and their magic gives no answer at all. — known some · told later · source D026, D070

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `prophecy.asked` *(Ink · GM-only)* After the rift, Rupiah asked the gods whether it would ever happen again. — known few · told later · source D025
- `prophecy.answer` *(Ink · GM-only)* The gods said yes: in hundreds of years of time and thousands of miles of distance, in the tiny fishing village of Kurose in Minkai. — known few · told later · source D025, D026, D048, D049
- `prophecy.conditions-not-right` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* Nobody knows when the next rift will come because the conditions for it aren't right yet, which is why augury and fortune-telling magic produce no answer. The players and the antagonists will bring together the right mix of things for it to happen. — known nobody · told later · source D077, D026

### The rift at Kortos *(event · 12 ink · 1 awaiting read · 2 pencil · 1 open · 5 GM-only)*

`rift` · threads: The founders

**What people know**

- `rift.opened` *(Ink)* About two hundred years ago, on the far side of the world, something opened in the air above the island of Kortos, near Absalom, and would not close. — known everyone · told from the start · when about 200 years ago · source D024, D025
- `rift.looked` *(Ink)* It was a violet light with a black heart. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, S001, D048
- `rift.grew` *(Ink)* It grew on whatever was near it: slowly at first, then faster, the rate itself slowly climbing, in fits and starts that made it deadly to study. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `rift.swallowed` *(Ink)* It absorbed many powerful priests, wizards and sorcerers who tried to stop it. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `rift.path` *(Ink)* It carved a jagged path across the island towards Absalom, changing direction seemingly at random. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `rift.converged` *(Ink)* Adventurers and magic-users converged to contain it, from across the island and then the whole region, among them the finest of Kortos's neighbouring states. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, S001, D048
- `rift.four-at-the-end` *(Ink)* Four people stood in front of it at the end. — known everyone · told from the start · source D025, D048
- `rift.uncertain-ending` *(Ink)* It was forced back and crushed into a small space, and either destroyed or changed into something else. Nobody who was there ever confirmed which. — known everyone · told from the start · source S001, D048
- `rift.nobody-knows-how` *(Ink)* Nobody agreed on what it was, or why it happened. — known everyone · told from the start · source D024
- `rift.histories-skip-the-start` *(Awaiting read)* The histories go from nothing to catastrophe and never say how it began. — known everyone · told from the start · source D027, episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `rift.entered-absalom` *(Ink)* It was stopped only after it had partly entered Absalom, cutting through a temple to Pharasma. — known everyone · told later · source D025

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `rift.cause` *(Ink · GM-only)* The four caused it, by accident: they fumbled a container of exotic fuel on the cargo deck of a crashed generation ship at Kortos, and it breached. — known few · told later · source D029, D032, D040, S001
- `rift.how-it-was-closed` *(Ink · GM-only)* Sarenrae sent the four back from Nirvana with a way to close it, and it worked because it was one dropped container. — known few · told later · source D040
- `rift.the-fumble` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* How First Impact began: on the generation ship's cargo deck, a clean throw got the container of fuel clear, and the catch failed, two attempts and two natural ones. The container split open. An "exhaling portal" opened, space curved, and a planar breach flung the four founders across the planes to Nirvana, leaving a violet aperture with a black core in the heart of the ship. When they came back, the rift had carved across Kortos into Absalom. — known few · told later · when 4721 AR · source D071, D030, D072, D031, D032, D081
- `rift.arrived-late` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* When the four came back from Nirvana the rupture was much larger, and they swung in to stop it expanding further. That is why they arrived late to their own disaster: they were on another plane while it grew. This is Ingram's working account, marked "presumably". — known few · told later · when 4721 AR · source D072, D030

Still hers: `rift.sarenrae-sent`.

`second-rift` · threads: The Watcher

Stopping it needs the mitflit home world, so the last part of the campaign is a journey by starship. — known nobody · told later · source D026, D070, D040, D081

- `second-rift.can-build` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* The Watcher is made of its makers' own nanomachines, so it can build what they built, and it builds its weapon from exotic matter without understanding that it could destroy the Watcher itself, the city, Golarion and a stretch of space around it. — known nobody · told later · source D071, D040, D081

- `second-rift.gap-is-after` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* The Gap is an event that happens after the adventure, perhaps as a result of it. ## §6 The world

### The age *(concept · 2 ink · 1 awaiting read · 5 pencil · 3 open · 5 GM-only)*

`era` · threads: The mayor and the police

**What people know**

- `era.two-hundred-years` *(Ink)* The rift at Kortos was about two hundred years ago, and the passage of time has changed much. — known everyone · told from the start · source D004, D024, S001
- `era.present-year` *(Ink)* The campaign's present is the year 4921 AR. — known everyone · told later · source D070
- `era.engines` *(Awaiting read)* Magic is still part of everyday life, small and cheap, but the great works of this age are built with engines: steam and oil, then electricity; railways across continents, steamships that don't wait for the wind, and wires carrying voices between cities. — known everyone · told from the start · source episode-c1e1--from-up-here
- `era.golarion-1950s` *(Pencil · Claude)* The setting is Golarion in its own 1950s-style retrofuturistic branch, with light, specific touches of real Golarion (temples of Pharasma, real ancestry terms, real place names such as Kortos and Absalom) where they serve the story, and no obligation to follow the rest. — known everyone · told later · source D077
- `era.fifties-feel` *(Pencil · Claude)* The setting reads as the 1950s, specifically of Japan: red-roofed old-town streets terraced up a cliff on one side, smokestacks and a more industrial waterfront on the other, aqueduct-like structures threading the city, and a sea-fort out in the channel, joined to the shore by a long causeway at the point through which the city's seaborne wealth passes. It is magic and fey beside industrial capitalism, giant machines and teenage drama, all at once. Ordinary society runs on roughly 1950s industrial capitalism, with tall sailing ships beside modern harbour craft, while Frame technology is narrow, scarce and institutionally controlled, derived from what was dug up. The two sit together in one harbour, and a Frame is far more advanced than the street it works in. — known everyone · told later · source D074, D081

**Secrets: only a few, or nobody, know** *(GM-only)*

- `era.dug-up-not-invented` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Ordinary society stayed at roughly a 1950s level while giant machines and out-of-era devices exist because the advanced technology was dug out of the two crashed ships, not invented: it is narrow and scarce, only partly understood even by the Directorate, and kept gated, which is why only trained pilots touch it. The phones run on the same ship-derived substrate, which is the only way anything with a phone's capability could be built in this era. The Directorate keeps the original ship's technology highly restricted to stop it destabilising the world, but it still leaks outwards from Kortos. — known few · told later · source D077, D032, D034
- `era.loosely-golarion` *(Pencil · hers · GM-only)* This world started as Golarion, but Ingram changed the mitflits, then Kortos island, then Abadar, so it is loosely based on Golarion and not a slave to it. The passage of time has changed much, and one of the most important events is First Impact. — known nobody · told later · source D078, D004
- `era.magic-draining` *(Pencil · Claude · GM-only)* Magic is slowly draining from Golarion, and industry has grown into the vacuum. That is the whole reason this world went from medieval to smokestacks in two centuries, and every long-lived character (Anabala, Shucks, Rupiah) has personally watched it happen. It explains the age, not the rift. — known few · told later · source D078, D040

Still hers: `era.tech-trickle`, `era.electronics-source`, `era.kortos-cataclysm`.

### Book III: The Reel
